name: connectdirect

corpus.note: Measured 2026-09-21 over 127 public GitHub COBOL repositories, 558,281 files, with diag/measure-rules.mjs --packs. Read the denominator before the number: every rule in this pack is JCL-scoped, and only 45 of the 127 repositories contain any JCL at all. WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW. It shows these rules are not broadly noisy - they do not fire on ordinary COBOL and JCL. It does not show they are quiet where they would actually run, because a public corpus of teaching material, vendor demos and tooling contains essentially no estate running this product. A rule that cannot fire for want of the product is not the same as a rule that sees the product and stays quiet, and this measurement cannot tell those apart. The practitioner review is still the half that would.

validation._note: Two different questions. A corpus measurement over public COBOL repositories tells you how often these rules fire, which is their noise. It cannot tell you whether the risk statements are true. Fill corpus with {repositories, firedOn, perRule} from diag/measure-rules.mjs --packs connectdirect; fill practitioner with {by, date, note} when someone who has run Connect:Direct has read it.

source: IBM Connect:Direct for z/OS User Guide and Process Language Reference. Process statements are submitted through DMBATCH, so they appear in JCL in-stream data rather than in any COBOL source.
coverage: Process language statements submitted through the batch interface: SIGNON, RUN TASK, RUN JOB, SUBMIT and COPY. Not covered: the Secure+ configuration, the network map, initialisation parameters, or anything whose risk depends on the node's own authorisation settings. Those live outside the repository.
why: Connect:Direct exists to move data off the platform, which makes every one of its processes an egress path by design. Two of its statements do more than move data: RUN TASK and RUN JOB execute code on the partner node. A repository that carries them carries remote execution.

rules.risk: executes a program on the partner node
rules.rationale: RUN TASK runs a program on the node at the other end of the transfer. It is remote execution written into a repository, and the machine it runs on is by definition one this repository does not control.

rules.risk: submits a job on the partner node
rules.rationale: RUN JOB submits JCL for execution on the partner node. Everything true of RUN TASK is true here, with the submitted job's own authority added to it.

rules.risk: carries a userid and password in the process
rules.rationale: A SIGNON whose USERID operand carries a second positional value is supplying a password in the process text. The credential is then in the repository, readable by everyone who can read it.
SNODEID supplies the security credentials used on the partner node. Like SIGNON with a password, a second positional value is a secret, and it is a secret for a system this repository does not own.

rules.risk: transfers a dataset to another node
rules.rationale: A COPY naming a secondary node moves data off this system. It is the ordinary purpose of the product rather than a defect, and it is listed at a severity that says so, because an egress path is worth seeing even when it is intended.

rules.risk: submits a further process from a dataset
rules.rationale: SUBMIT runs another Connect:Direct process named by a dataset. What that process does is decided elsewhere, so the reachable behaviour of this job is not visible in this job.

DMBATCH is how a job talks to Connect:Direct at all, and it is named on the EXEC statement rather than in the process text below it. It is not itself a finding; it is listed so a reader can see which jobs reach the product, which is the inventory question that precedes every other rule in this pack.
